content:
Reports indicate that code discovered in the camera app of the latest iOS 27 beta appears to point to the introduction of several major professional photography and videography features.

Although the built-in camera app has gradually gained more features over time, for an app primarily designed for casual point-and-shoot use, this discovery comes as somewhat of a surprise…

Apple has always tried to strike a balance between the two—on one hand making its own camera app extremely easy to use for taking snapshots, while on the other hand offering a degree of creative control for users who want to use it as a serious camera. However, despite the app gradually evolving, most photography and videography enthusiasts still tend to prefer third-party apps.

If this discovery holds true, the introduction of some powerful features usually associated with professional cameras could well change the landscape. Developer pdfu says he has found code supporting four major features, none of which have been enabled in any current beta version.

Exposure Assistance Tools

Judging exposure by eye is often highly unreliable, especially when viewing the iPhone screen in bright sunlight. Most professional cameras support a histogram function to accurately display exposure status, while video editing software tends to use a waveform as an alternative display method. Pdfu says he has already located the relevant code for these two features in the beta version.

Focus Peaking

How much of a photo remains in focus from the closest foreground to the farthest background depends on several factors, but in certain shooting situations only part of the scene will be sharp. Likewise, judging by eye which areas are in focus and which are not is not entirely reliable, which is why professional-grade video cameras in particular adopt a method called focus peaking.

When this feature is enabled, an overlay can be activated to highlight the areas that are in focus, usually in red—though the example on the left uses yellow instead.

Highlight Clipping Warning

The biggest risk posed by exposure errors is overexposure. Generally speaking, if shadows are underexposed, they can often be rescued in post-processing—unless the situation is extremely severe, shadows will rarely go completely black (i.e., RGB values of zero). Overexposure is far more serious, because it is easy to completely "blow out" the highlights, meaning they exceed an RGB value of 255 and cannot be recovered in post.

Many professional cameras use what's called a zebra pattern indicator, with red diagonal stripes marking areas that are completely blown out. Some cameras also let you manually set the threshold for this warning, so you can be alerted when approaching overexposure (e.g., 90%) rather than only when actual blow-out occurs.

This feature is also shown on the right side of the image above.

Manual Focus

Currently, while the camera app can lock focus on a specific element in the frame, it must simultaneously lock the exposure for that point as well via AE/AF lock (auto exposure/auto focus).

The report indicates Apple has been testing a true manual focus feature operated via a slider within the camera app. According to Pdfu, this feature may be limited to one or more upcoming new iPhone models.

Other Features

Beyond the professional features, an option reportedly being added is the ability to take a burst of multiple timed self-portraits. Often when people want to take a group photo they want to take several shots; this feature would let everyone set the iPhone on a tripod or another surface, then capture a series of photos and pick one that everyone is happy with.

Lastly, there are also indications that a new image processing method will be adopted, to accommodate the variable aperture design we expect to appear on the iPhone 18 Pro.

9to5Mac's Take

None of the features mentioned above have been enabled in any iOS 27 beta version so far. I would be surprised if Apple puts these features into the built-in camera app rather than restricting them to Final Cut Camera—but the report does seem quite credible.

What are your thoughts on this report? Feel free to share your opinions in the comments section.
